Pr eface
Robert G. Frank and T imothy R. Elliott
Mor e than 20 years ago, we (T im Elliott and Bob Frank) began to work on the first edition 
of the Handbook of Rehabilitation Psychology . For several years, we had chatted about  
the pr ogr ess in our field and the need to consolidate knowledge in one compr ehensive, 
contemporar y text. W e shar ed a common vision of oppor tunities for the field, i n c l u d i n g  
a need for gr eater theor etical development, the value of the scientist–practitioner as a 
metamodel encouraging adaptive thinking as a discipline, and the need for str onger r ecog -
nition of the changing models of health car e on psychologist practice. In 1995, we began to 
outline curr ent knowledge and ar eas in which we hoped to inspir e futur e gr owth. By 1997, 
we set to work in earnest to bring together leaders in the field to craft a compendium of 
knowledge defining the discipline and its potential for the futur e. It took 3 years to r ealize 
our vision: The first edition was published in 2000, at the dawn of a new centur y .
Rehabilitation psychology was in an exciting phase at that point as the discipline struggled 
to become a specialty and to integrate the momentous changes occurring in the lar ger health 
car e envir onment. In our final chapter “After wor d: Drawing New Horizons” (Elliott & Frank, 
2000), we consider ed the pr omise of the centur y in light of the status of the field of r ehabili -
tation psychology . This “look for war d” to consider issues the discipline needed to addr ess 
in the near and distant futur e focused on pr ofessional identity , the impor tance of integrating 
r ehabilitation psychology into the lar ger changes in health car e and science, and the need to 
move away fr om “naïve empiricism” that dominated the literatur e at that point. Our think -
ing r eflected a distinct bias towar d the value of the “scientist–practitioner model” as the most 
critical element of gr owth for r ehabilitation psychology . W e r ecognized the impor tance of 
r ehabilitation psychologists engaging in national experiments to cr eate alternative health car e  
deliver y models focused on cost-ef fective, integrated car e for all aspects of people’ s lives 
(physical, psychological, functional, envir onmental) and whatever challenges they faced. 
W e noted the likely transformative power of new brain imaging models su c h a s f u n c t i o n a l 
magnetic r esonance imaging to change assessment and our understanding of brain–behavior 
r elationships. W e concluded that psychologists must be catalysts in changing the focus fr om 
acute car e to integrated car e addr essing chr onic health limitations and psychological health.
As the first compilation of exper t perspectives on theor y , r esear ch, and clinical practice 
in r ehabilitation psychology , the first edition of this handbook quickly became the primar y 
r esour ce for the discipline. In 2004, T im Elliott suggested the need for a second edition r eflect -
ing the pr ogr ess of the field, though he would not be able to par ticipate. Mitch Rosenthal had 
pr eviously appr oached Bob Frank indicating his inter est in being involved in futur e editions of 
the handbook, so he joined the team, r eplacing T im. A few weeks later , Bruce Caplan joined us

as thir d editor . By 2007 we had the pr oject on track. However , in May of that year , we and our 
colleagues ar ound the world in r ehabilitation psychology wer e stunned by Mitch’ s untimely 
death. Given our close friendship and his significant r ole in managing the development of a 
number of chapters in the second edition, we lost a year r ecovering fr om his death and coming 
to terms with the need to push the pr oject for war d without his involvement. The second edit i o n 
of the Handbook of Rehabilitation Psychology was published in 2010.
W e asked one of the truly innovative thinkers in the field of r ehabilitation psychology , 
John Corrigan, to write the last chapter of the second edition. In his chapter , “After wor d:  
Of Bins and Arr ows” (Corrigan, 2010), he r ecognized the histor y of theor etical fragmentation 
that Elliott and Frank (2000) described as “naïve empiricism” disconnected fr om theor etical 
models. Corrigan described the phenomenon as “bins” of theor y that “did not inform each 
other , but rather sat side-by-side as competing models” (Corrigan, 2010, p. 477). He noted 
that the development of the W orld Health Or ganization’ s International Classification of 
Functioning, Disability and Health (2000) was impor tant for cr eating critical “bins” for  
r ehabilitation psychology with the inclusion of health and function, and for cr eating an 
overar ching model that highlighted influences between the bins. Pointing to the scientific 
advances that occur when r esear ch focuses on interactions of multiple influences on behavior , 
Corrigan (2010) pr ovided the example of the incr easing impor tance of understanding  
genotypic expr ession as a function of envir onmental influences. He noted that phenotypic 
plasticity , the dif fer ential expr ession of genotypic expr ession as a function of the envir onment, 
potentially interacts with the bins af fecting behavior and may cause plasticity to be expr essed 
within the lifetime of an or ganism (Corrigan, 2010). Corrigan fur ther r eflected on the value 
of r esear ch on interactions between bins as exemplified in the gr owing inter est in applying 
“big data” (i.e., sifting thr ough lar ge databases to identify r elationships) to understand how 
envir onmental factors in neighbor hoods impact health and social well-being. For example, 
Corrigan and Bogner (2008) found that neighbor hood characteristic impr oved pr edictions  
of subjective well-being among individuals with traumatic brain injur y . Corrigan (2010) 
concluded, “It may be time to look beyond disability and chr onic illness as complex condi -
tions with multiple interactions and attend to ways these influences interact and influence 
with each other in their own right” (p. 480).
As the second edition aged, we began to consider the need for a thir d edition r eflecting 
changes within the field. T im Elliott r eturned as a coeditor , and we r ecognized a need to  
better r eflect the dynamics of the Division of Rehabilitation Psychology . Lisa Br enner and 
Stephanie Reid-Arndt agr eed to join our team, adding their experience and perspectives 
r eflecting the best and brightest of the new demographic of the Division of Rehabilitation 
Psychology . The thir d edition of the Handbook of Rehabilitation Psychology addr esses a 
mor e matur e specialty , now r ecognized by the AP A Council of Specialties. The number of 
individuals with Diplomates in r ehabilitation psychology has rapidly moved to match the 
numbers of much mor e historic specialties. 
As noted by John Corrigan (2010) in his conclusion to the second edition, r ehabilitation 
psychology incr easingly inter faces with the health of the population. Population health  
r ecognizes multiple determinants of health outcomes, “including medical car e, public health 
inter ventions, aspects of the social envir onment (income, education, employment, social  
s u p p o r t , cultur e) and of the physical envir onment (urban design, clean air and water),  
genetics, and individual behavior” (Kindig & Stoddar t, 2003, p. 381). Recognizing the 
changing emphasis on health outcomes and the need to understand multiple determinants 
of health, the thir d edition includes chapters on public health, global health, community

r ehabilitation, and the epidemiology of disability . Recognizing the many new technologies 
impacting r ehabilitation, chapters on ar tificial intelligence and technology changes in r ehab

As with the pr evious edition of the handbook, appr oximately 30% of the material in the 
thir d edition is new to the volume, and the r emainder is dedicated to updated content on 
foundational issues such as spinal cor d injur y , traumatic brain injur y , acquir ed disability , 
amputation, burn injuries, chr onic pain, and disability associated with aging. The thir d edit i o n 
also pr ovides curr ent guidance r egar ding education and training, health policy , ethics, and 
various r oles that r ehabilitation psychologists face in assessment, inter vention, critical car e, 
and consultation.

Standards of Accr editation T raining and Practice Competencies for Doctoral Graduate, Inter nship,  
and Postdoctoral Residency Pr ograms (Revised July 2017)
Discipline-specific knowledge
Categor y 1: Histor y and Systems
Understanding and knowledge of the origins and development on major ideas in psychology
Categor y 2: Basic Content Areas in Scientific Psychology
Understanding and knowledge of the basic content areas in psychology including the five contents areas: affective aspects of beh avior , 
biological aspects of behavior , cognitive aspects of behavior , developmental aspects of behavior , and social aspects of behavior
Categor y 3: Advanced Integrative Knowledge in Scientific Psychology
Understanding and demonstrating advanced integrative knowledge of multiple basic discipline-specific content areas (listed in  
Categor y 2)
Categor y 4: Research Methods, Statistical Analysis & Psychometrics
Understanding and demonstrating advanced integrative knowledge of rese ar ch methods, statistical analyses, and psychometrics
Professionwide competencies
Understanding and demonstrating advanced integrative and independent ability to formulate and conduct resear ch or other scholarly 
activity , and critically evaluate and disseminate resear ch and scholarship that contributes to the knowledge base
Understanding of and competency in professional ethical and legal standards and laws, recognize ethical dilemmas that may  
occur and apply ethical decision-making processes to resolve these, and conduct self in an ethical manner in all professional 
activities
Understanding of and competency in individual and cultural diversity , relevant theories and the empirical knowledge base, ability 
to work effectively with others from diverse background and identities, and be able to integrate awareness of their own personal 
attitudes may affect how they understand and interact with others
Understanding and demonstrating professional values and attitudes (including int egrity , deportment, professional identity , lifelong 
learning, self-reflection, responsiveness to feedback, and overall professiona l effectiveness) in complex situations and with appro -
priate degree of independence
Understanding and demonstrating professional communication and interpersonal skills (including maintenance of effective relat ion -
ships, ability to produce and comprehend verbal, nonverbal, and written communication for various audiences) across academic, 
social and professional arenas, and an ability to manage difficult commu nications well
Understanding of and competency in diagnostic classification systems, c lient strengths and psychopathology , and psychological 
assessment practices grounded in the best available empirical literature, wit hin appropriate contexts, accurately interpreting and 
effectively communicating assessment results orally and in writing to app ropriate audiences
Understanding and demonstrating competency with psychological inter ventions and associated literature base, utilizing evidence-
based approaches effectively , and modifying these approaches consistent with ongoing evaluation and as indicated
Understanding of and competency in super vision models and practices
Understanding and demonstrating competency with consultation models and practices, and demonstrating knowledge and respect for 
the roles and perspectives of other professions

T ABLE 5.2
Adapting Inter ventions Based on Clinical Pr esentation
Area of impairment Strategy
Motor function ■ ■ Coach individuals with impaired hand function to use voice-activated sma rtphone programs to access 
online tools such as relaxation apps.
■ ■ Consider telehealth deliver y models when transportation is a barrier .
Attention ■ ■ Assess potential inter ference from auditor y or visual stimuli and minimize distractions.
■ ■ When individuals have a short attention span, present information in smalle r “chunks,” break down  
complex tasks, stop and review , and ask patient to repeat back.
■ ■ Focus on one topic at a time and one task at a time (listen, then take notes).
■ ■ Provide written session outline/summar y at beginning.
■ ■ Provide in-session breaks or conduct shorter sessions.
Memor y ■ ■ Ask about preferred memor y compensator y tools (e.g., notebook, digital recorder , photos, video record -
ings, voice-activated dictation) and encourage their use within sessions.
■ ■ When individuals do not complete homework, provide reminder calls or te xts, or set up smartphone 
reminders to prompt completion of assignments.
■ ■ With permission, include family members in sessions to provide between- session support (e.g., cues, 
reminders to carr y out homework).
■ ■ With problems encoding new information, provide more learning trials, encourage patients to focus on 
key words, and use visual imager y and semantic context (forming stories) to enhance learning.
■ ■ With problems retrieving learned information, use retrieval practice to aid r ecall.
■ ■ Encourage patient in session to summarize and highlight main points in materials, and make summar y notes.
■ ■ Post instructional video demonstrating task.
Language ■ ■ For individuals with receptive language impairments, use simple concrete t erms and minimize jargon.
■ ■ Use gestures, pictures, and graphics to reinfor ce verbal communication.
■ ■ Stop and confirm understanding frequently .
■ ■ Emphasize therapy options that are less language dependent (e.g., physic al activity or behavioral activa -
tion for depression vs. cognitive restructuring).
■ ■ For individuals with expressive language impairments, make use of augm entative and alternative commu -
nication devices (e.g., alphabet, picture boards, dr y erase board, computerized communication systems).
■ ■ Ask yes or no questions; determine the most reliable means of responding.
Processing speed ■ ■ Speak slowly and present information at slower rate, discuss with patien t, and calibrate accordingly .
■ ■ Allow more time to formulate responses.
Executive function ■ ■ When individuals are tangential, agree on a signal to indicate conversation is off topic.
■ ■ When individuals are perseverative, negotiate strategies to interrupt proce ss and explicitly practice  
turn-taking in conversations.
■ ■ For individuals who have difficulty sequencing and shifting cognitive sets, f ocus on one topic at a time; 
signal when switching topics.
■ ■ For individuals who think concretely , make interpretations and recommendations explicit and direct.
■ ■ When individuals have difficulty with generalization, model and role-play pr oblem-solving behavior .
■ ■ Dedicate multiple sessions to generalization of tasks and relapse prevention.
Impulsivity ■ ■ Develop and practice metacognitive script (e.g., before action: stop, think , then act).
Initiation/motivation ■ ■ Include support person in treatment planning and implementation.
■ ■ Make greater use of scheduled activity and practice.
■ ■ Establish cues and reminders for sessions (e.g., reminder call), and activities (e.g., phone alarms, prompts).
■ ■ Focus on tasks that are intrinsically rewarding and aligned with goals.
Fatigue ■ ■ Schedule sessions at times when patient is most alert.
■ ■ Have shorter , more frequent sessions.
Emotion regulation ■ ■ Model calm composed behavior , problem solving, and interpersonal communication.
■ ■ Include explicit focus on distress tolerance skills.

T ABLE 7.5
Clinical Evaluation and T r eatment: Underlying Functional Competencies and Skills in the American 
Psychological Association Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct
Functional skills  
and stages Functional competencies
Beneficence and Nonmaleficence
Initial inter view/ Introduce the person with disability (PWD) to the rehabilitation process, a nd what to expect, in appropriate 
evaluation language.
Ensure that the PWD’ s welfare is safeguarded and varied rights and responsibilities within the health care 
environment are explained and protected.
Ensure that all rehabilitation psychology practices adhere to and comply with federal and state statutes and 
regulations, as well as health care organization policies and procedures.
Assessment Be knowledgeable of and using current evidence-based assessment meth odologies appropriate to the PWD’ s 
health condition.
Identify benefits and limitations of tools selected and the resulting information and determining the PWD’ s 
understanding of these.
T reatment  Ensure that rehabilitation psychology and other team planned inter ventions are intentionally designed to 
planning benefit the PWD within her or his personal, health, family and social support system, and community 
environmental contexts.
Ensure attention to risk reduction regarding the PWD’ s health, lifestyle, emotional, behavioral, cognitive, 
educational, vocational, and social contexts.
Inter vention Coordinate rehabilitation psychology ser vices with other team treatment ser vices to facilitate enhanced health, 
functional per formance, welfare, and safety of the PWD.
Ensure that risk reduction has been demonstrated as a treatment outcome metric.
Discharge  Demonstrate how treatment outcome goals are met.
planning Understand whether functional status meets self- and/or assisted care capa city , consistent with a safe return 
to the community .
Incorporate plans to minimize risk on return to the community .
Fidelity and Responsibility
Initial inter view/ Establish the parameters of the working relationship between the rehabilit ation psychologist and rehabilitation 
evaluation team and the PWD.
Identify barriers to building rapport.
Engage in consultative discussions with team members and other health c are practitioners as required by  
the needs of the PWD.
Ensure the PWD’ s understanding of the roles and responsibilities of a rehabilitation psychologist and other 
associated team members.
Assessment Resolve potential conflicts among team members regarding who assesse s what.
Establish the PWD’ s understanding of the uses of resulting data for treatment planning in the team treatment 
milieu.
Provide the PWD with feedback and ensure that he or she understands the personal and programmatic  
implications of test data, including a rationale for normative comparisons.
T reatment  Represent the PWD’ s goals regarding rehabilitation psychology ser vices in the rehabilitation team treatment plan.
planning Ensure the PWD’ s per formance commitment regarding goal achievement within the treatment plan.
Inter vention Facilitate the consistent constructive participation of the PWD in the treatm ent process across all rehabilita -
tion inter ventions.
Determine reasonable per formance progression toward goal achievement within or above the expected range 
for program continuation toward completion.
Manage personal stresses affecting treatment effectiveness.

and stages Functional competencies
Discharge  Lay out a plan for continuity of care based on rate of recover y , ongoing care and treatment needs and  
planning availability of resour ces.
Demonstrate adaptive relationships with the PWD and caregivers that fos ter ongoing rehabilitation ser vices as 
required.
Integrity
Initial inter view Demonstrate open and accurate discussions of the workings of the rehabilit ation team evaluation and  
and evaluation treatment process.
Establish the baseline of the PWD’ s understanding of his or her health condition and supporting realistic 
expectations regarding recover y trajector y and rehabilitation treatment outcome in the context of personal, 
familial, and social cir cumstances.
Assessment Identify potential barriers to valid assessment, including engagement by the PWD.
Demonstrate accurate test administration and interpretation within the co ntext of the PWD’ s health status and 
individual needs.
Ensure timely documentation of a written test interpretation summar y .
T reatment  Demonstrate episodic treatment plan updates and responsiveness to the PWD’ s questions regarding treatm e n t 
planning plan status and goal achievement progress.
Ensure that the PWD has an accurate understanding of team per formance metrics and implications for  
functional applications to the home and community environment.
Inter vention Demonstrate treatment adjustments on the basis of sufficient and accurate PWD awareness of per formance status 
that influence decision making regarding the complexity of information disclosures and nature of activities to 
help the PWD maintain focus and effort on goal attainment.
Discharge  Ensure the PWD and caregivers (per the PWD’ s consent) have an accurate and thorough understanding of 
planning current health needs, along with an accurate prognosis of the continuing recover y course.
Support use of a broad range of functional, cognitive, emotional, and behavioral outcome metrics to enhance 
the quality of rehabilitation program care.
Justice
Initial inter view/ Determine fair distribution of time.
evaluation Use current evidence-based practices and standards relevant to the PWD’ s presenting health issues.
Assessment Recognize the impact of disability on assessment and implement appropr iate accommodations in support of 
access to assessment tools.
Ensure the PWD’ s understanding of the use of assessment across peers and diagnostic populations,  
if applicable, in the context of provision of rehabilitation ser vices.
T reatment  Demonstrate advocacy for personal goals and methods of goal achievem ent regarding community integration 
planning by means of agency and resour ce access, including planning for continuity of care after discharge from 
rehabilitation ser vices.
Inter vention Identify supplementar y treatment resour ces and ensure that all PWDs ser ved receive adequate material 
resour ces, information, recommendations, and assistance to optimize functional per formance in the  
rehabilitation process.
Discharge  Anticipate postdischarge access issues and addressing barriers (e.g., emot ional, cognitive) to maximize 
planning likelihood of following up on any needed ongoing treatment, care, or social assistance through community-
based agencies.
Advocating for equitable access should barriers to required treatment an d care.

Respect for People’ s Rights and Dignity
Initial inter view/ Implement safeguards to protect the rights of individuals whose autonomous decision making is impaired.
evaluation Determine the PWD’ s comprehension of information.
Demonstrate awareness of biases affecting personal responses to the PWD; a nd respect for diversity  
represented in the disability culture; as well as diversity represented in et hnic, racial, cultural or other  
differentiating factors.
Establish an advocacy role on behalf of the PWD when concerns or conflicts arise and regarding community 
reentr y .
Assessment Identify disability concerns related to garnering permission for assessme nt.
Explain parameters of confidential records, release of information, and pr ivacy rights.
Ensure the PWD’ s understanding of these as well as normative data comparisons accounting for relevant 
diversity issues.
T reatment  Ensure that the PWD’ s self-identified health needs are addressed; integrate inter view and evaluation and 
planning assessment data in the contexts of health histor y , expressed personal needs/preferences, and social  
environmental cir cumstances.
Provide the PWD with sufficient information to make informed decisions regarding the treatment plan and 
community reintegration; alternatively , ensure that assistance and super vision regarding decision making  
is established for PWDs who have limited decisional capacity .
Inter vention Demonstrate understanding of a PWD’ s decision-making rights.
Ensure the PWD understands his or her rights to participate in decisions regarding directing and modifying 
the treatment process, along with the right to refuse treatment.
Incorporate sensitivity to and relevance of cultural, individual, and role di fferences in treatment processes.
Set treatment outcome goals that reflect those characteristics.
Discharge  Support appropriate PWD control over use of health records by means of release-of-information procedures.
planning Ensure optimal self-determination within an appropriate level of independ ent daily living as determined by the 
PWD’ s strengths, challenges, and support network.
Note . PWD = person with a disability .

relationships

family roles

Inter vention Provides education about disabilities and how to navigate barriers within systems
